questions.explanation: A row filter or column mask is a function attached to a single table. ABAC policies apply filters and masks wherever a governed tag appears, across many tables. Dynamic views, using functions such as is_account_group_member(), are the older pattern that the other two improve on.

questions.question: An audit finds that some agent requests are missing from the inference table. What's a likely explanation?
choices: Payloads larger than 1 MB aren't logged to inference tables
Requests from users in other regions are logged separately
Inference tables keep only a random 10% sample of requests
Inference tables drop requests that the model answered quickly
questions.explanation: Inference tables are Unity Catalog Delta tables that log requests and responses through governed endpoints, but payloads over 1 MB aren't logged. If audits need large payloads, log them another way, for example with MLflow tracing.

questions.question: A security lead says, 'Agents that can call tools are impossible to govern.' What's the accurate reply on Databricks?
choices: Unity Gateway governs MCP services, UC functions and HTTP connections, with policies and logging
Tool calls are safe by default because every tool call is checked by a human before it runs
Tools are governed only when the agent runs in Genie, never when it runs on Agent Runtime or Apps
That's right: tool calls bypass Unity Catalog, so the only safe choice is agents with no tools at all
questions.explanation: Unity Gateway covers MCP services, Unity Catalog functions and HTTP connections as well as models. It adds usage tracking, inference tables, rate limits, guardrails for PII and prompt injection, and Contextual Service Policies that can allow, deny or require approval. Governance is built in rather than bolted on.

questions.question: An agent on Databricks Apps uses user authorization and calls Genie for the signed-in user. Whose permissions apply when Genie queries the data?
choices: The app's service principal, for every user
The signed-in user's, passed through by the app
The workspace admin who deployed the app
The SQL warehouse owner who pays for compute
questions.explanation: With user authorization, the app acts as each signed-in user (it receives the user's token, for example through the x-forwarded-access-token header, within the scopes the app declares). Genie and Unity Catalog then see that user, so row filters and column masks apply.

questions.question: An agent calls an external model through Unity Gateway. Where can you later see the request and its cost?
choices: Only in MLflow experiments created by the developer
Nowhere, because external calls leave Databricks
Only in the external provider's own billing console
Requests and responses in inference tables, and spend in system tables
questions.explanation: Unity Gateway can log requests and responses to inference tables in Unity Catalog, and usage and spend land in system tables, with external provider estimates in system.ai_gateway.external_model_spend. That gives one place to audit and charge back, even when the model lives elsewhere.

questions.question: Before an external model endpoint can call OpenAI from Databricks, what has to be set up?
choices: Nothing, because Databricks includes OpenAI usage in every workspace's DBUs
A Databricks-hosted copy of the OpenAI model, deployed on provisioned throughput endpoints
The provider's API key, stored centrally and encrypted, which the endpoint references
A Fabric connection, because external models route through Microsoft's network
questions.explanation: External model endpoints route to third-party providers using credentials you supply, stored centrally and encrypted rather than in notebooks. The provider bills the usage, and Unity Gateway can add limits, logging and guardrails on top.

questions.question: Which features does Learn list for Lakebase?
choices: Vector-only storage with no SQL interface, designed for embeddings and similarity search
Only nightly batch exports to Delta, with no branching, autoscaling or point-in-time restore
Autoscaling, scale to zero, branching, instant restore, read replicas, high availability and synced tables
A columnar warehouse engine that replaces Databricks SQL warehouses for BI workloads
questions.explanation: Learn lists autoscaling, scale to zero, branches for dev and test, instant restore from any point in the history window, read replicas, high availability with failover, synced tables and Unity Catalog registration.

questions.question: What do Lakebase synced tables do?
choices: Replicate Postgres tables to Microsoft Fabric OneLake automatically, so Power BI can query them in Direct Lake mode
Copy Lakebase tables to SharePoint lists every hour for business users
Merge every Postgres database in the account into one shared table
Sync Unity Catalog tables into Lakebase so applications can query them at low latency
questions.explanation: Synced tables bring curated lakehouse data into Postgres for low-latency app and agent lookups. The reverse direction, Change Data Feed (Public Preview), stores Postgres row changes as Unity Catalog Delta tables.

questions.question: How does Learn suggest agents use Lakebase?
choices: As the place where model weights are stored and loaded by agents at runtime, replacing Model Serving for small models
It doesn't; Lakebase is only for BI dashboards
As a replacement for Unity Catalog permissions
As a state store holding durable short- and long-term memory, for example for LangGraph agents
questions.explanation: Learn calls Lakebase 'a state store for agents' that holds durable short- and long-term memory for agents built with LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK. It's also an online feature store for Model Serving.

questions.question: What does Lakebase's Change Data Feed (Public Preview) do?
choices: Emails admins each time a row changes
Streams Delta table changes into Postgres in real time
Sends Postgres changes to Microsoft Dataverse
Stores Postgres row changes as Unity Catalog Delta tables
questions.explanation: Change Data Feed captures Postgres row changes into Unity Catalog Delta tables, so operational data written by apps and agents lands in the lakehouse for analytics and governance. It's in Public Preview.

questions.question: How are Databricks Apps billed?
choices: Per request, with no charge while the app is idle
Per user per month, like a seat license that's assigned to each person who opens the app
They're free; Apps compute is included in every workspace
Per hour of compute while the app is running, based on its provisioned capacity
questions.explanation: Apps are billed per hour of compute while running, based on provisioned capacity. An idle app that's left running still costs money, so stop dev apps. Databricks also limits the number of apps per workspace.

questions.question: Which workspace tier do Databricks Apps require?
choices: Premium
Standard
Enterprise only, with an add-on license
Any tier, including the Free Edition trial
questions.explanation: Learn says Databricks Apps require a Premium tier workspace.

questions.question: Which compute sizes do agents on Databricks Apps support?
choices: Medium and large only
Small only
Extra-large only
Any size, including GPU
questions.explanation: The authoring page lists only medium and large compute sizes for agents on Databricks Apps. Factor that into cost estimates for always-on agents.

questions.question: A developer runs 'databricks bundle deploy' for an agent app but the old version is still running. Why?
choices: bundle deploy only uploads and configures; 'bundle run' starts or restarts the app
bundle deploy works only for Node.js apps
Apps update only once a day at midnight UTC, so the new version appears the next morning
The developer needs workspace admin rights for deploys to take effect
questions.explanation: The authoring page notes that bundle deploy uploads and configures, and bundle run is required to start or restart the app. bundle run takes the YAML key, not the app name.

questions.question: When should a team pick a storage-optimized AI Search endpoint over a standard one?
choices: For small indexes that need the lowest possible latency and the highest query rate, since storage-optimized is the premium tier
Only when the data is stored in Microsoft Fabric
For over a billion vectors, when faster indexing matters more than about 250 ms of extra latency
Whenever the index uses Direct Vector Access
questions.explanation: Standard endpoints hold about 320 million vectors at dimension 768 and support high QPS. Storage-optimized holds over a billion, indexes 10 to 20 times faster and adds about 250 ms of query latency, with pricing optimized for large vector counts.

questions.question: What's the difference between a Delta Sync index and a Direct Vector Access index?
choices: They're the same; the names differ only between clouds
Delta Sync is for images and Direct Vector Access is for text
Direct Vector Access syncs automatically from a Delta table; Delta Sync requires manual updates through the REST API
Delta Sync tracks a source table; Direct Vector Access is updated through the REST API
questions.explanation: Delta Sync indexes track a source table (Delta, streaming, materialized view or managed Iceberg v3) automatically, with Databricks-computed or self-managed embeddings. Direct Vector Access needs manual updates through the REST API and is supported only on standard endpoints.

questions.question: What does a standard AI Search endpoint require on the source table for a Delta Sync index?
choices: Nothing; any table works
Change data feed enabled (row tracking enables it automatically)
A primary key that's an integer column, plus liquid clustering on the text column
Liquid clustering on the embedding column
questions.explanation: Standard endpoints need change data feed on the source table so the index can sync incrementally. Row tracking enables it automatically.

questions.question: A team creates an AI Search index from a small source table, then loads far more data. What can go wrong?
choices: The index switches to Direct Vector Access
The source table is truncated
Capacity is provisioned from the source size at creation, so they may hit capacity-exhausted errors
Nothing, because AI Search capacity always grows automatically with the source data at no extra cost or delay
questions.explanation: Index capacity is provisioned based on the source size at creation, so a small start can cause capacity-exhausted errors later. Size indexes for expected growth.

questions.question: Which privilege do you need to create an AI Search index?
choices: CAN MANAGE on every endpoint in the workspace
Account admin
CREATE TABLE on the target schema
MODIFY on the source table
questions.explanation: Indexes are Unity Catalog objects, so creating one needs CREATE TABLE on the schema. Endpoints are governed by access control lists, and Databricks recommends a service principal for production.

questions.question: What's the difference between ai_query and task-specific AI Functions such as ai_extract or ai_classify?
choices: ai_query is free; task-specific functions are billed per seat
ai_query calls a model endpoint you choose; task functions use Databricks-managed systems for one job
ai_query is for Python notebooks only, and task-specific functions work only in SQL warehouses running on Classic compute
There's no difference; they're aliases
questions.explanation: ai_query is the general-purpose function for model flexibility. Task-specific functions (ai_parse_document, ai_extract, ai_classify, ai_summarize, ai_translate, ai_mask and others) run on Databricks-managed serverless infrastructure tuned for each task.

questions.question: Can AI Functions run on a Classic SQL warehouse?
choices: Yes, and they're cheapest there because Classic warehouses don't bill for inference
Yes, but only ai_query
No; use a pro or serverless SQL warehouse or supported compute
Only on weekends
questions.explanation: The AI Functions page says they aren't available on Classic SQL warehouses. The compute running the query is always billed, on top of model inference.

questions.question: What does Databricks recommend for running AI Functions over a large dataset?
choices: Export the data to Excel first
Run each row by hand in the AI Playground
Split the data into thousands of small queries in a Python loop, so each call stays under the rate limit
Submit the full dataset in a single query, and run production work in pipelines, jobs or streaming
questions.explanation: Databricks says to submit the full dataset in one query rather than splitting it manually, and to productionize with Lakeflow pipelines, jobs or Structured Streaming. An AI Function task (Beta) in jobs processes only new or changed inputs.

questions.question: What does ai_parse_document take and return?
choices: A table name in; a vector index out
A SharePoint site ID in; a list of file names, owners and sensitivity labels out, ready for indexing in AI Search
A URL in; a plain-text summary out
Binary file content in; a VARIANT of typed elements (text, tables, figures) with bounding boxes out
questions.explanation: It takes BINARY content for PDF, JPG/JPEG, PNG, TIFF, DOC/DOCX and PPT/PPTX and returns a VARIANT with elements such as text, tables (as HTML), figures, titles and headers, each with confidence and a bounding box.

questions.question: Which limits apply to ai_parse_document?
choices: No limits
English only, with no images
10 pages per document and 1 MB per file, with English text only and no support for images or scanned pages
500 pages without a page range, 100 MB per file and no custom models
questions.explanation: Documents over 500 pages fail without a pageRange, files are capped at 100 MB and custom models aren't supported. Non-Latin text such as Japanese or Korean is handled less well, and digitally signed documents may not process accurately.

questions.question: How can a team cut the cost of ai_parse_document when they don't need figure descriptions?
choices: Run it on a Classic SQL warehouse, which has no inference cost
Set descriptionElementTypes to an empty string
Use version 1.0 of the function
Convert all PDFs to images first
questions.explanation: Setting descriptionElementTypes to '' skips AI-generated figure descriptions and reduces cost and compute. It's a simple lever for large document backlogs.

questions.question: Which embedding models can a Knowledge Assistant's AI Search index use?
choices: databricks-gte-large-en, databricks-bge-large-en or databricks-qwen3-embedding-0-6b
Any OpenAI embedding model, through an external model endpoint in Unity Gateway
Only Microsoft's text-embedding-3 models
Any model, because Knowledge Assistant re-embeds everything
questions.explanation: When Knowledge Assistant uses an existing AI Search index, the index's embedding model must be one of these three Databricks-hosted models.

questions.question: Which index type supports full-text search in Databricks AI Search?
choices: Only indexes created through Genie
Any Direct Vector Access index on a standard endpoint
A full-text index on a storage-optimized endpoint, in Beta
None; AI Search is vector-only
questions.explanation: The docs list a full-text index type (Beta) that requires a storage-optimized endpoint and triggered sync. Hybrid queries are capped at 200 results versus 10,000 for ANN queries.

questions.question: What are Databricks AI Functions?
choices: Serverless functions that run when a file lands in a Unity Catalog volume
SQL functions that apply AI to data at scale, such as ai_query, ai_extract and ai_classify
Prebuilt chat agents that answer questions about the functions in a workspace
Python decorators that turn any function into an agent tool and register it in Unity Catalog automatically
questions.explanation: AI Functions bring AI into SQL. ai_query calls any supported model endpoint, and task functions such as ai_extract, ai_classify, ai_summarize and ai_parse_document run on Databricks-managed systems. You pay for the query's compute plus inference for most functions.

questions.question: An agent needs to remember each user's preferences and conversation state across sessions, with fast reads and writes. Which Databricks service fits?
choices: A Unity Catalog volume of JSON files
A Delta table read through a SQL warehouse
An AI Search Direct Vector Access index
Lakebase
questions.explanation: Lakebase is Databricks' managed Postgres with autoscaling, scale to zero and branching, and it's a natural home for agent memory and app state. Analytical warehouses and file volumes aren't designed for many small, low-latency reads and writes.

questions.question: An agent needs to find similar past support tickets among millions, by meaning rather than exact words. Which service fits?
choices: A metric view over the tickets table
A Genie Agent with the tickets table added
A Databricks AI Search index kept in sync with the tickets table
A Lakebase synced table of the tickets
questions.explanation: AI Search (formerly Vector Search) does vector and full-text search, and a Delta Sync index stays in sync with its source table. Genie writes SQL, which is great for counts and trends but not for 'find tickets like this one'. Note that AI Search indexes don't support row- or column-level security.

questions.question: What's the difference between Lakebase and a Databricks SQL warehouse?
choices: Lakebase stores only vector embeddings for search; a SQL warehouse stores every other kind of table in the lakehouse
They're the same engine with two prices: Lakebase is simply the serverless edition of a Databricks SQL warehouse
Lakebase runs analytics over lakehouse tables; a SQL warehouse is managed Postgres for fast transactional reads and writes
Lakebase is managed Postgres for fast transactional reads and writes; a SQL warehouse runs analytics over lakehouse tables
questions.explanation: Lakebase is an operational (OLTP) Postgres database: app state, agent memory, low-latency lookups, with synced tables bringing lakehouse data in. A SQL warehouse is analytical compute for SQL and BI over Delta tables, and it's what Genie and dashboards run on.

questions.question: What's the difference between AI Search and Genie?
choices: AI Search writes SQL over governed tables; Genie finds documents by meaning for retrieval
They're the same engine: Genie is the chat interface on top of an AI Search index
AI Search is for business users in Teams; Genie is a developer API with no user interface
AI Search finds content by meaning; Genie turns questions into SQL over governed tables
questions.explanation: AI Search (formerly Vector Search) is a retrieval service: vector and full-text search over indexed content, used inside agents. Genie answers analytical questions by writing SQL against Unity Catalog tables and metric views. Many agents use both: retrieval for documents, Genie for numbers.

questions.question: An agent's retrieval step returns passages from documents that some users shouldn't see. The index is an AI Search index. Why?
choices: The agent uses the wrong embedding model, which ignores the table's row filters
AI Search indexes don't support row- or column-level security, so they return whatever they hold
AI Search applies row filters only to the first 1,000 results that it returns for each query a user sends
AI Search checks each user's permissions only when the index is rebuilt each night
questions.explanation: AI Search indexes are governed in Unity Catalog as objects, but they don't support row- or column-level security. Control what goes into each index, split indexes by audience, or filter results by user attributes in the agent's code.

questions.question: What does Genie's per-user monthly free allowance cover?
choices: Genie's LLM usage only; compute such as serverless SQL is billed separately
Nothing; the allowance is a discount on the Databricks platform commitment instead
Everything Genie does, including the SQL warehouse compute used to run each query
Only Genie Code; Genie One and Genie Agents are billed per seat from the first question
questions.explanation: The Genie pricing page says free usage applies to Genie LLM usage only, and Genie compute (for example serverless SQL) is billed separately. Model the warehouse cost of a Genie rollout even while LLM usage is free.

questions.question: Genie's pricing page says the free allowance is 150 DBUs. What's the dollar figure, and is it the same everywhere?
choices: $1.50, and it's the same in every region
$30 in every region, to match the Microsoft 365 Copilot list price
$150 per user per year in every region, paid up front
About $10.50 in US East, and the dollar equivalent varies by region
questions.explanation: The pricing page footnote says 150 DBUs equals $10.50 in US East and that the dollar equivalent varies by region. Databricks' blog rounds it to 'up to $10 of free usage per user every month'.

questions.question: When did Genie Code move to pay-as-you-go billing?
choices: January 31, 2027, together with Genie One and Genie Agents
June 1, 2025, at a flat $20 per developer per month
July 8, 2026, with a per-user free monthly allowance
It hasn't; Genie Code is free for all users with no end date
questions.explanation: Learn says that starting July 8, 2026, Genie Code is billed pay-as-you-go with a per-user free monthly allowance. The promotion that makes Genie One and Genie Agents free through January 31, 2027 doesn't mention Genie Code.

questions.question: A customer pilots Genie Agents with 800 users in December 2026. What should they budget for?
choices: Nothing at all, since compute, LLM usage and service principal calls are all free until January 31, 2027
$30 per user per month from the first day of the pilot
Warehouse compute and service principal usage now, and LLM usage after January 31, 2027
A one-time Genie activation fee per workspace
questions.explanation: Genie One and Genie Agents usage by users is free through January 31, 2027, but service principals are excluded and compute is billed separately. Build the post-promotion LLM cost into the business case so the pilot doesn't hide the run rate.

questions.question: How do you turn a Foundation Model API rate in DBUs into dollars?
choices: Multiply by the Microsoft 365 Copilot credit rate
Divide by 1,000, because one DBU always costs one tenth of a cent everywhere
Multiply the DBU rate by the $/DBU price of the SKU in the customer's cloud and region
You can't; FMAPI prices are published only in dollars
questions.explanation: Databricks pricing pages give rates in DBUs (for example per million tokens) and say final price = SKU $/DBU × DBU rate. The page's example uses $0.07 per DBU, an AWS US East price; Azure prices differ, so use the customer's contract rate.

questions.question: Llama 3.3 70B pay-per-token input is listed at 7.143 DBUs per million tokens. How many DBUs do 100 million input tokens use?
choices: About 71,430 DBUs
About 2,143 DBUs
About 714 DBUs
About 7 DBUs
questions.explanation: 100 million tokens is 100 × 1 million, so 100 × 7.143 = 714.3 DBUs. Output tokens are billed separately at 21.429 DBUs per million. At the page's $0.07 example rate, that's about $0.50 per million input tokens.

questions.question: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Databricks pay-per-token is listed at 42.857 DBUs per million input tokens and 214.286 per million output tokens. What does that imply?
choices: Input and output tokens cost the same, so answer length doesn't matter for cost
Output tokens cost five times as much as input tokens, so verbose answers drive cost
Only output tokens are billed; input tokens are free
Input tokens cost five times as much as output, so long prompts are the main cost
questions.explanation: 214.286 ÷ 42.857 = 5. Output-heavy agents (long reports, verbose reasoning) cost much more than retrieval-heavy ones. Capping output length and choosing concise formats are real cost controls.

questions.question: Using Databricks' listed pay-per-token input rates, how does Claude Sonnet 4.5 compare with Llama 3.3 70B?
choices: About 60 times as expensive
About the same price, because Databricks charges one flat rate per million tokens for every hosted model
About six times as expensive (42.857 versus 7.143 DBUs per million input tokens)
Cheaper, because proprietary models are discounted
questions.explanation: 42.857 ÷ 7.143 = 6. Routing simple classification or extraction steps to an open-weight model and reserving frontier models for hard reasoning is the main cost lever. Unity Gateway routing and evaluation make it safe to test.

questions.question: When does Databricks recommend provisioned throughput over pay-per-token for Foundation Model APIs?
choices: Only for embeddings; chat models can't use it
For every prototype and dev workload, because provisioned throughput is always cheaper per token than pay-per-token
Never; provisioned throughput was retired in 2026
For production work that needs performance guarantees, custom weights or certain compliance needs
questions.explanation: Pay-per-token is the recommended starting point. Provisioned throughput fits production workloads needing performance guarantees, fine-tuned or custom weights, or compliance such as HIPAA. It's billed per hour for provisioned model units and requires serverless compute.

questions.question: What is priority pay-per-token on Foundation Model APIs?
choices: A reserved capacity contract that must be bought a full year in advance, in exchange for guaranteed response times
An opt-in per request ('priority' service tier) with no commitment but a higher per-token rate
A discount for customers who spend more than $1 million a year
The default tier for every request
questions.explanation: Priority mode is opt-in on each request with service_tier set to 'priority'. It needs no commitment and costs more per token. Make sure developers don't set it by default.

questions.question: How is Foundation Model API provisioned throughput priced?
choices: Per million tokens, exactly like pay-per-token, with a volume discount once monthly usage passes a threshold
Per user per month
Per question answered
In DBUs per hour for provisioned model units, some only on reservations
questions.explanation: Provisioned throughput is sold in model units and priced in DBUs per hour. Some frontier models show only one- or three-month reservation pricing. Hourly billing means utilization matters: idle provisioned capacity is still paid for.

questions.question: What does enabling regional processing (data residency) do to the price of eligible Databricks-hosted models?
choices: Makes them free
Adds a 10% uplift on marked models
Nothing; residency is free on every model
Doubles the price
questions.explanation: The pricing page says marked models get a 10% uplift when regional processing is enabled. Factor that in when regulated customers require in-region inference.

questions.question: What are the cost layers when you run AI Functions in SQL?
choices: The compute running the query, plus model inference for most functions
A flat monthly fee per function used
Only a per-seat Databricks SQL license, with no usage charges for the queries
Only inference; compute is free for AI Functions
questions.explanation: The compute running the query is always billed. Most task-specific functions bill inference separately, and ai_query bills the serving endpoint it targets. ai_forecast, ai_detect_anomalies, ai_predict_class, ai_predict_value and ai_top_drivers run with no separate inference cost.

questions.question: In system.billing.usage, under which product do ai_extract, ai_classify and ai_parse_document show up?
choices: MODEL_SERVING with BATCH_INFERENCE
SQL
AI_FUNCTIONS
GENIE
questions.explanation: The AI Functions page maps ai_classify, ai_extract, ai_parse_document and ai_search to AI_FUNCTIONS. ai_query and functions such as ai_summarize, ai_translate and ai_mask appear as MODEL_SERVING with BATCH_INFERENCE. Knowing this matters when building cost dashboards.

questions.question: For batch ai_query jobs, which models does Databricks recommend?
choices: External models through Azure OpenAI only
Provisioned throughput endpoints, always, because batch jobs need reserved capacity to finish
Custom GPU endpoints only
Databricks-hosted models (the 'databricks-' endpoints) rather than provisioned throughput
questions.explanation: The AI Functions page recommends Databricks-hosted models with the 'databricks-' prefix over provisioned throughput for batch ai_query.

questions.question: Which spend does a Unity Gateway budget cover?
choices: Every Databricks charge, including clusters, storage, SQL warehouses and provisioned throughput endpoints
Pay-per-token, AI Functions, Genie and optionally external models, not provisioned throughput
Only Copilot Credits
Only external providers such as OpenAI
questions.explanation: Budgets cover pay-per-token, AI Functions, Genie and (in Beta) external model providers. They don't cover provisioned throughput or standalone Model Serving endpoints, which need other controls.

questions.question: What actions can a Unity Gateway budget take when a threshold is reached?
choices: Downgrade every user to a smaller model
Send email, block usage or (in Beta) trigger a webhook
Automatically buy more DBUs
Only send email to admins; blocking usage isn't possible
questions.explanation: Email alerts only, and users keep access. Block usage enforces: users see an exhausted-budget message until the period resets or an admin raises the threshold. Webhooks are in Beta. Only the highest shared threshold can block.

questions.question: A CFO wants Unity Gateway budgets to guarantee that the billed amount never exceeds $50,000. What does Databricks say?
choices: Budgets cancel the Databricks contract when exceeded
Budgets are exact to the cent and guarantee the cap, because each request is checked against billing before it runs
Enforcement is approximate, so don't rely on it for an absolute cap on billed amounts
Budgets refund any overage automatically
questions.explanation: The budgets page says enforcement is approximate: users may be blocked early, spend can exceed the threshold before enforcement, and in-flight requests aren't stopped. It says not to use budgets to ensure an absolute cap. system.billing.usage is the source of truth.

questions.question: How do per-user thresholds work in a Unity Gateway budget?
choices: The lowest applicable override always wins
Limits that apply only to service principals
One lifetime limit per user that never resets, with overrides where the lowest applicable threshold always wins
Daily and monthly per-user limits, with user or group overrides; the highest applicable one applies
questions.explanation: Per-user thresholds can be daily, monthly or both, with overrides for users or groups; the highest applicable threshold for each period applies. Daily limits reset at 00:00 UTC and monthly on the first of the month.

questions.question: Which limits and roles apply to Unity Gateway budgets?
choices: One budget per workspace, managed only by account admins, with no per-user thresholds or delegated roles of any kind
4 shared thresholds and 100 overrides per budget, 1,000 budgets per account; Budget Manager and Viewer roles
Unlimited budgets, each managed by any user
Budgets can only be set through a support ticket
questions.explanation: Each budget can have four shared thresholds and 100 per-user overrides, and an account can have 1,000 budgets. Account admins, workspace admins (for their workspaces) and delegated Budget Manager or Budget Viewer roles can manage them. Developers can check their limits with 'ug usage'.

questions.question: Which table does the budgets page call the source of truth for spend?
choices: system.billing.usage, which updates every few hours
Inference tables
The Azure portal's Copilot billing page
A CSV file that Databricks emails to account admins monthly
questions.explanation: system.billing.usage is the source of truth and updates every few hours. External provider estimates come from system.ai_gateway.external_model_spend, which updates hourly.

questions.question: How are custom model and GPU serving endpoints billed?
choices: In DBUs per hour of provisioned compute, not per token
Free, since custom models aren't billed
Per token, like pay-per-token models, at a discount for GPUs
Per seat
questions.explanation: Custom CPU and GPU endpoints are billed in DBUs per hour; for example, the pricing page lists one H100 GPU at 100 DBUs per hour. Utilization and scale-to-zero settings drive the cost.

questions.question: What caveat do Databricks pricing pages give about model prices listed for a region?
choices: Prices are fixed for five years from the date of the customer's contract
Prices include Microsoft 365 licensing
Prices apply only to US customers
Displayed prices don't guarantee the product is available in that region
questions.explanation: The pages say displayed prices don't guarantee availability in a region. Pay-per-token and provisioned throughput availability differ by region, so check the region page before quoting a design.

questions.question: A 5,000-person company expects about 600 people to ask data questions each month. How does Genie's pricing model affect cost compared with per-seat tools?
choices: Genie charges a flat enterprise fee regardless of usage
Genie charges per table, so user count doesn't matter
There are no seats, so cost tracks actual users and usage, with a free allowance per user
Every employee must be licensed, so the cost is the same as per-seat tools regardless of usage
questions.explanation: Genie has no seat-based pricing: each user gets a monthly free allowance and pays for usage beyond it, with compute billed separately. Per-seat tools charge for every licensed user whether or not they ask questions.

questions.question: How can a FinOps team break down AI spend in Unity Gateway?
choices: Only by workspace, with no user-level, model-level or tag-level detail
Only through monthly PDF invoices
It can't; AI spend isn't tracked
By model, principal and tag, using usage tracking in system tables
questions.explanation: Unity Gateway provides cost analysis by model, principal and tag, built on system tables. Tag agents and use cases at creation so chargeback works later.

questions.question: What is serverless compute in Databricks?
choices: Compute that runs on users' laptops and syncs results back to the workspace
Compute that runs in the customer's own cloud account, configured and sized by a workspace admin
Databricks-managed compute that starts quickly, scales automatically and bills by usage
A free tier of compute that Databricks gives every workspace for testing
questions.explanation: Serverless compute is managed by Databricks, so there are no clusters to configure. It's available for notebooks, jobs, pipelines and SQL warehouses, starts in seconds and bills by usage. Classic compute runs in the customer's own cloud account.

questions.question: What are Databricks Foundation Model APIs?
choices: A catalog of third-party model providers that Databricks resells under a single monthly subscription per user
Databricks-hosted models, open and proprietary, served through endpoints and billed pay-per-token by default
Tools for training a new foundation model from scratch on the customer's own data and GPUs
A directory of public model APIs that agents can call without any credentials or governance
questions.explanation: Foundation Model APIs serve hosted models such as Llama, GPT, Claude and Gemini through endpoints with the databricks- prefix. Pay-per-token is the default, priority pay-per-token costs more per request, and provisioned throughput reserves capacity by the hour.

questions.question: A Unity Gateway budget is set to block usage, yet costs from a provisioned throughput endpoint keep growing. Why?
choices: Budgets cover provisioned throughput, but only after 30 days
Budgets block usage only on weekends, when most batch jobs run
Unity Gateway budgets don't cover provisioned throughput, which needs other controls
The endpoint's owner is exempt from every budget they create
questions.explanation: Budgets cover pay-per-token, AI Functions, Genie and, optionally, external models. They don't cover provisioned throughput or standalone Model Serving endpoints, which are billed by the hour. Control those through sizing, scale-to-zero and who can create endpoints.

questions.question: During Genie's free usage period, finance sees Genie AI charges from one workload: a nightly job that calls the Conversation API as a service principal. Why?
choices: The charges are for Genie Code, which every API call is billed as
Service principals don't get free usage and are billed at standard pay-as-you-go rates
The job ran outside business hours, which the free period doesn't cover
The free period covers only questions asked in the Genie One app, not calls made through the API
questions.explanation: Databricks excludes service principals from Genie's free usage and bills them at standard pay-as-you-go. Running a shared workload as a service principal also weakens per-user Unity Catalog enforcement. Budget for service principal usage separately.

questions.question: A CFO says, 'Per-seat AI is easier to predict, so it must be cheaper.' What's the accurate reply?
choices: Seats are predictable but bill every licensed user; usage pricing tracks real use and can be capped
Predictability doesn't matter, because AI costs are too small to appear in an annual budget
Usage pricing is always cheaper because vendors never charge for compute when users ask questions
That's right: per-seat pricing is always cheaper because vendors discount seats far more than they discount usage
questions.explanation: Per-seat pricing buys predictability, but you pay for every licensed user whether they use the tool or not. Genie has no seats: each user gets a free monthly allowance and pays for usage beyond it, with compute billed separately, and Unity Gateway budgets can alert or block. The right answer depends on how many people will really use it.

questions.question: A user asks a Genie Agent a question. Which costs does that one question create?
choices: A per-question fee charged to the Genie Agent's creator
Only Genie's AI usage, because warehouse compute is included
Only the SQL warehouse compute, because Genie's AI is always free
Genie's AI usage, counted against the user's allowance, plus SQL warehouse compute for the query
questions.explanation: Each question uses Genie's AI, which draws on the user's monthly free allowance (and is free through January 31, 2027 for users), and runs SQL on a warehouse billed in DBUs. Model both when sizing a rollout, and watch warehouse sizing as usage grows.

questions.question: After Genie's promotion ends, 600 users each use about $14 of Genie AI a month. Assuming a $10 free allowance per user, what's the monthly AI cost, before compute?
questions.explanation: Each user is $4 over the allowance, and 600 × $4 = $2,400 a month. Warehouse compute is billed separately. The allowance is 150 DBUs, about $10.50 in US East, so the dollar figure varies by region.

questions.question: An agent uses 50 million input tokens and 5 million output tokens of Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Databricks (42.857 DBUs per million input, 214.286 per million output). About how many DBUs is that?
choices: About 1,071 DBUs
About 12,857 DBUs
About 2,143 DBUs
About 3,214 DBUs
questions.explanation: Input: 50 × 42.857 ≈ 2,143 DBUs. Output: 5 × 214.286 ≈ 1,071 DBUs. Total ≈ 3,214 DBUs. Output is a third of the bill from a tenth of the tokens, so capping answer length matters. Multiply by the customer's $/DBU rate for dollars.

questions.question: A custom model runs on one H100 GPU endpoint, listed at 100 DBUs per hour, around the clock for 30 days. How many DBUs is that?
choices: 2,400 DBUs
3,000 DBUs
72,000 DBUs
questions.explanation: 100 DBUs × 24 hours × 30 days = 72,000 DBUs. GPU endpoints bill by the hour whether or not requests arrive, so scale-to-zero and right-sizing are the main cost levers for spiky workloads.

questions.question: What does OpenAI's help center list as ChatGPT Business seat prices in most countries?
choices: $60 per user per month with a 150-seat minimum and a mandatory annual commitment
Free for up to 50 users, then $10 per user per month billed monthly
A single $30 seat billed annually, with no monthly option and no premium tier for heavy users
Standard $20 per user per month annually or $25 monthly; Premium $100 annually or $125 monthly
questions.explanation: OpenAI's ChatGPT Business overview lists Standard seats at $20 annual or $25 monthly and Premium seats (higher usage limits) at $100 annual or $125 monthly. Pricing can vary by country and currency. Enterprise is 'contact sales'.

questions.question: What was ChatGPT Business called before August 29, 2025?
choices: ChatGPT Pro
ChatGPT Team
ChatGPT Work
ChatGPT Enterprise Lite
questions.explanation: OpenAI says ChatGPT Team was renamed ChatGPT Business on August 29, 2025. ChatGPT Work is the agent experience included in Business and Enterprise.

questions.question: What does OpenAI say ChatGPT Enterprise admins get for audit and retention?
choices: No audit capability; conversations can't be exported or retained by the company
A monthly PDF report of the top prompts in the workspace
An audit log of conversations and GPTs through the Compliance API, and admin control of retention
Audit through Microsoft Purview only, for tenants that also buy Microsoft 365 E5 or E7 licenses
questions.explanation: OpenAI's enterprise privacy page says admins can access an audit log of conversations and GPTs through the Enterprise Compliance API and control retention; deleted conversations are removed within 30 days. It also lists SAML SSO, AES-256 at rest and SOC 2 Type 2.

questions.question: What can ChatGPT Business and Enterprise customers buy when users need more than their seats include?
choices: Credits for more access, on top of seat fees
Copilot Credits from Microsoft
Nothing; seats are unlimited for every user
Additional seats only, since credits don't exist
questions.explanation: OpenAI's pricing page says Enterprise and Business can purchase credits for more access. Like Microsoft's Copilot Credits, it's a seat-plus-usage model, so heavy agent use has a variable cost on top of the seat.

questions.question: How is Claude Enterprise priced on Anthropic's pricing page?
choices: A flat $60 per seat per month with unlimited usage and no minimum
$30 per seat per month, matching Microsoft 365 Copilot, with usage included
A $20 per seat per month fee billed annually, 20-seat minimum, plus usage at API rates
Free seats; customers pay only for API tokens through a cloud marketplace
questions.explanation: Anthropic lists Claude Enterprise as a seat price plus usage at API rates: $20 per seat per month billed annually, a 20-seat minimum and an annual commitment. Usage cost scales with model and task, so budget it like metered consumption.

questions.question: Which governance features does Anthropic list as Enterprise-only, not in the Claude Team plan?
choices: Claude Code and Claude for Microsoft 365
Projects and connectors
Single sign-on and central billing, which Team leaves out because it's aimed at small groups
SCIM, role-based access, audit logs, the Compliance API and custom data retention
questions.explanation: Anthropic's plan table shows Team with SSO, central billing and connector admin controls, but no SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, Compliance API or custom retention. Those, plus a HIPAA-ready offering, are Enterprise features.

questions.question: Which data controls does Anthropic highlight for Claude Enterprise?
choices: Data stored in the customer's SharePoint
Custom data retention, customer-managed encryption keys and US-only inference
EU-only inference for every plan, including Free, with no option for US-only processing
On-premises deployment of Claude models
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Enterprise page lists custom data retention, customer-managed encryption keys and US-only inference, plus IP allowlisting. It also says inputs and outputs aren't used for training by default.

questions.question: Which seat types and sizes does Anthropic list for the Claude Team plan?
choices: 2 to 150 users; Standard seats at $20 annual or $25 monthly, and Premium seats with 5x usage
Minimum 500 users, billed only by invoice, with a single seat type and no monthly billing option at all
Unlimited users at a single $40 seat with no premium option
1 to 10 users, free
questions.explanation: Team is for 2 to 150 users. Standard seats are $20 per month annually or $25 monthly; Premium seats are $100 annually or $125 monthly with 5x more usage. Team also includes up to $500 per month in pooled API credits.

questions.question: How does Claude connect to internal systems in Team and Enterprise plans?
choices: It can't connect to any internal systems
Prebuilt connectors such as Google Drive, Slack and Microsoft 365, plus custom MCP connectors
Only through Microsoft Graph connectors
Only through file uploads, since Anthropic doesn't offer connectors to internal systems in Team or Enterprise plans
questions.explanation: Anthropic lists prebuilt connectors and custom connectors via MCP for internal systems. MCP is the common thread across Claude, Databricks managed MCP, Snowflake and AWS AgentCore, so a Genie MCP server can reach many front ends.

questions.question: Which Gemini Enterprise editions does Google's editions page list?
choices: Business, Standard, Plus, Frontline and a pay-as-you-go edition
E3, E5 and E7
Free, Pro and Ultra, matching Google's consumer plans for individuals
Starter, Growth and Scale
questions.explanation: Google lists Business (1 to 500 users), Standard, Plus, Frontline (requires 150 or more Standard or Plus users) and Pay-as-you-go (one-seat minimum, billed from prepaid credits or invoice). Pooled storage per user rises from Business to Plus.

questions.question: What gotcha does Google's editions page note about Gemini Enterprise seat credits and partner models?
choices: Seat credits cover every model, including partner models such as Claude, with no pay-as-you-go option above quota
Partner models are free for Plus edition customers
Seat credits cover first-party Gemini models only; partner models like Claude are pay-as-you-go
Partner models aren't available in any edition
questions.explanation: The footnotes say included monthly seat credits apply strictly to first-party Gemini models, partner models (Anthropic Claude) are billed pay-as-you-go, license editions must turn on pay-as-you-go usage above quota, and usage is subject to a monthly spend limit.

questions.question: Which prebuilt connectors does Google's Gemini Enterprise overview name?
choices: Only BigQuery and Looker
Only Google Workspace apps, with no third-party connectors
Confluence, Jira, Microsoft SharePoint and ServiceNow
None; all connectors must be custom
questions.explanation: The overview names Confluence, Jira, SharePoint and ServiceNow, and Google's launch blog mentions Microsoft 365, Salesforce and SAP. Like Copilot and ChatGPT, Gemini Enterprise competes for the 'front door' to company knowledge.

questions.question: How does AWS price Amazon Bedrock AgentCore?
choices: Per user per month, like a productivity suite seat with included usage
Consumption-based, per component, with no upfront commitment or minimum fee
Per agent per month, regardless of usage
A flat annual platform fee per AWS account
questions.explanation: AgentCore pricing is consumption-based with no upfront commitments or minimum fees. Components (Runtime, Browser, Code Interpreter, Gateway, Policy, Identity, Memory, Observability, Evaluations and more) are each metered separately, so costs add up across services.

questions.question: How is AgentCore Runtime billed?
choices: Per agent deployed, per month
Per user who chats with the agent
Per million tokens processed by the agent, including tool calls
Per second of vCPU-hours and GB-hours of memory, with a one-second minimum
questions.explanation: Runtime runs agents in microVMs billed per second for vCPU and memory. Model tokens, Gateway calls, Memory, Observability (CloudWatch) and Evaluations are separate meters, so an AgentCore estimate has many lines.

questions.question: When is AgentCore Identity free, and how is Observability billed?
choices: Both are billed per agent per day
Identity is free through Runtime or Gateway; Observability is billed at CloudWatch rates
Identity is billed per user per month; Observability is free
Both are always free, because AWS includes identity and observability in every AgentCore Runtime charge
questions.explanation: AgentCore Identity charges per 1,000 token or API key requests for non-AWS resources but is free through Runtime or Gateway. Observability isn't an AgentCore rate; it's charged through CloudWatch pricing.

questions.question: How does AWS price Quick (formerly marketed as Amazon Quick Suite) for organizations?
choices: Per dashboard per month
Purely per token with no seats or account fees, billed through the customer's existing Bedrock usage
Per user per month by edition, with agent hours, plus a $250 monthly account fee
A free add-on to every AWS account
questions.explanation: Organization plans are Essentials ($3), Professional ($20, 8 agent hours per user) and Enterprise ($40, 18 agent hours), plus a $250 per account per month infrastructure fee. Extra agent hours cost $3 each, metered per second.

questions.question: How are Snowflake Cortex Agents billed?
choices: Per agent per month, with tokens included
Free with any Snowflake edition
AI Credits per million tokens, with warehouse compute for generated SQL billed separately
Per user per month, with warehouse compute and tokens included, so the cost doesn't change with usage
questions.explanation: Snowflake bills Cortex Agents in AI Credits per million tokens. The warehouse compute that runs generated SQL is billed separately, and Cortex Search adds serving and embedding costs. It's a layered cost model, much like Genie's LLM usage plus SQL compute.

questions.question: What does Snowflake charge per AI Credit?
choices: It varies by user count
Free for Enterprise edition
$2.00 with global routing or $2.20 with regional routing, regardless of edition
$3.00 for every edition, the same as a standard Enterprise platform credit
questions.explanation: AI Credits are separate from platform credits and cost the same regardless of edition: $2.00 with cross-region (global) routing enabled and $2.20 with regional routing. Data residency choices therefore change the price.

questions.question: Which Snowflake Cortex Agent tools send requests over the public internet?
choices: None; every tool stays inside Snowflake
Cortex Search
Cortex Analyst
Web search and MCP connectors
questions.explanation: Snowflake's Cortex Agents docs say web search (enabled at account level) and MCP connectors send requests over the public internet. Ask the same question about every platform's external tools.

questions.question: What does Cortex Analyst use to turn questions into SQL?
choices: Semantic views that define business metrics and entity relationships
Power BI semantic models
Raw tables only, with no semantic layer
Unity Catalog metric views shared into Snowflake through Delta Sharing
questions.explanation: Cortex Analyst generates SQL over semantic views, Snowflake's semantic layer. Unity Catalog metric views play the equivalent role for Genie. Snowflake recommends calling Cortex Analyst through Cortex Agents.

questions.question: How is Cortex Search billed?
choices: Per query at a flat $0.01
Serving compute per GB per month plus embedding tokens, at the regional AI Credit price
Per user per month
It's free with Cortex Agents, because search serving is included in the agent's per-million-token AI Credit rate
questions.explanation: Cortex Search is billed on serving compute (credits per GB per month) plus embedding tokens, at the regional AI Credit price regardless of the routing setting.

questions.question: How much does one Agentforce action cost under Salesforce's Flex Credits model?
choices: 20 Flex Credits, about $0.10, with Flex Credits sold at $500 per 100,000
$2 per action
Actions are free; only users are billed
One credit, about $0.005, with credits sold at $500 per million
questions.explanation: Flex Credits cost $500 per 100,000, and a standard action draws 20 credits (about $0.10). A voice action draws 30. Unused credits don't roll over, and overages are billed monthly in arrears at the contracted rate.

questions.question: What's Salesforce's per-conversation price for Agentforce, and what's the restriction?
choices: Free for the first million conversations
$0.10 per conversation, usable alongside Flex Credits, with the first million conversations included free
$2 per conversation for customer-facing agents; not in the same org as Flex Credits
$2 per conversation for employee agents only
questions.explanation: Conversations cost $2 each and apply to customer-facing agents. The FAQ says Flex Credits can't be used in the same org as Conversations, so the pricing model is an org-level decision.

questions.question: What do Salesforce's Agentforce add-ons for Sales or Service cost, and what do they include?
choices: They're free with any Salesforce license
$5 per user per month with unlimited customer conversations
$150 per user per month with unmetered employee usage
$550 per org per month with no usage limits
questions.explanation: Agentforce add-ons (Sales, Service, Field Service) are $150 per user per month with unmetered employee usage. The $5 Agentforce User License needs Flex Credits, and Max Edition starts at $550 per user per month with 2.75 million Flex Credits per org per year.

questions.question: What hidden cost do Salesforce's Agentforce pricing examples exclude?
choices: Data 360 (Data Cloud) credits
Flex Credits
Per-user licenses
Nothing; the examples are all-in
questions.explanation: Salesforce says its examples don't include other costs such as Data 360 credits. Ask what data platform consumption sits behind any agent price.

questions.question: How does Glean describe its product, and does it publish prices?
choices: An enterprise AI platform with permission-aware search and agents; prices aren't published
A Microsoft-owned search add-on for SharePoint at $5 per user per month, included in Microsoft 365 E5
A data warehouse for agent memory, priced per GB
A free open-source search engine
questions.explanation: Glean markets an enterprise AI platform with agents and '275+ app connectors' for permission-enforced search. Its pages offer demos rather than prices. Databricks itself is listed as a Glean customer.

questions.question: Which vendors in this deck combine a seat fee with metered usage for heavy or agentic work?
choices: Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT, Gemini Enterprise and Microsoft 365 Copilot
None; every vendor in this deck includes unlimited usage within the seat price
Only Snowflake
Only Databricks Genie
questions.explanation: Claude Enterprise adds usage at API rates; ChatGPT sells extra credits; Gemini Enterprise turns on pay-as-you-go above quota; Microsoft bills agentic work in Copilot Credits. Genie, by contrast, has no seat and a per-user free allowance, and Snowflake and AgentCore are purely consumption-based.

questions.question: What does Snowflake's Cortex Agents documentation say about access control?
choices: Agents run as ACCOUNTADMIN, so no grants are needed beyond access to the Snowsight UI and the agent's URL
Anyone with the agent's URL can query it
A Cortex role (CORTEX_USER or CORTEX_AGENT_USER) plus privileges on the agent and its tools' objects
Access is controlled only by Microsoft Entra groups
questions.explanation: Calling an agent needs SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER or SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_AGENT_USER plus privileges on the agent and on the objects its tools use. Like Genie with Unity Catalog, data access follows the platform's own roles.

questions.question: A sales team wants an agent that updates opportunities and logs calls inside Salesforce's own interface. Which platform fits that job best?
choices: A Databricks AI/BI dashboard embedded in Salesforce, with a writeback button added for updates
Salesforce Agentforce, with Databricks supplying governed analytics where it's needed
AWS Quick, since it's the only platform that can act on Salesforce records
A Genie Agent, which can update Salesforce records from inside the Genie One app
questions.explanation: Agentforce is Salesforce's agent platform and works natively on Salesforce records and workflows. Genie is strongest at governed questions over data. Recommending the right tool for an in-app CRM job, and showing where Databricks adds value, keeps your credibility with the customer.

questions.question: Which Snowflake capability is the closest equivalent to a Genie Agent?
choices: Snowpark Container Services, which hosts apps
Snowflake Marketplace, which shares datasets
Cortex Analyst, which writes SQL over semantic views
Cortex Search, which retrieves unstructured data
questions.explanation: Cortex Analyst turns natural-language questions into SQL over semantic views, much as a Genie Agent does over Unity Catalog tables and metric views. Cortex Search is Snowflake's retrieval service, closer to AI Search, and Cortex Agents orchestrate the two. Snowflake bills warehouse compute for generated SQL separately, like Databricks.

questions.question: A competitor shows a benchmark in which its agent beats everyone. How should you respond, given Databricks publishes its own benchmark too?
choices: Point out that only Databricks' benchmark is truly independent, so the competitor's results can be ignored
Agree that benchmarks settle the question, and recommend whichever vendor scored highest
Treat every vendor benchmark as a prompt to run a head-to-head on the customer's own data and questions
Avoid the topic, since accuracy doesn't matter for agents that answer data questions
questions.explanation: Databricks reported 84.5% first-attempt accuracy for Genie against 52.4% for the strongest general-purpose agent it tested, but that's a vendor benchmark too. The credible move is to propose a bake-off on the customer's data. Genie benchmarks make that easy to run and repeat.

questions.question: 100 people on AWS Quick Professional ($20 a user, 8 agent hours included each) use 10 agent hours each in a month. With a $250 account fee and $3 per extra agent hour, what's the monthly bill?
questions.explanation: Seats: 100 × $20 = $2,000. Account fee: $250. Extra hours: 100 users × 2 hours × $3 = $600. Total: $2,850. Seat-plus-usage pricing means heavy users push the bill past the seat count.

questions.question: An Agentforce deployment runs 30,000 actions a month. At 20 Flex Credits per action and $500 per 100,000 Flex Credits, what does that cost?
questions.explanation: 30,000 × 20 = 600,000 Flex Credits, and 600,000 ÷ 100,000 × $500 = $3,000, about $0.10 per action. Data 360 consumption is extra, so ask what else each action touches.

questions.question: A retailer wants 3,000 store managers to ask sales questions in natural language, each seeing only their own region. What's the strongest Databricks design?
choices: A Supervisor Agent that calls a shared service principal and trims rows in Python afterwards
A Genie Agent over metric views, used with each manager's identity so Unity Catalog row filters apply
A custom agent on Databricks Apps using app authorization, with region filtering written into the prompt
A Knowledge Assistant over weekly PDF exports of the sales reports, one folder per region
questions.explanation: Genie evaluates data access as the end user, so Unity Catalog row filters enforce regions without custom code, and metric views give consistent definitions. App authorization or a shared service principal would give everyone the same access unless code re-implements security.

questions.question: A customer asks, 'How do we know Genie will be accurate enough before rollout?' What's the best answer?
choices: Let users try it for a month and count complaints
Rely on Databricks' published benchmark of 84.5%, which applies to every customer's data and schema without further testing
Ask the model to rate its own confidence on each answer
Build benchmarks with varied phrasings and SQL answers, measure accuracy, then tune and rerun
questions.explanation: Genie benchmarks (up to 500 questions) measure accuracy on the customer's own data, with Chat mode comparing results to SQL answers and Agent mode using an LLM judge. Vendor benchmarks are a starting point; the customer's own benchmark is the evidence.

questions.question: Developers across 40 teams are calling frontier models through Databricks, and spend is rising. What's the first control to put in place?
choices: Ask teams to report their usage in a monthly spreadsheet
Ban frontier models and allow only open-weight models for every team, since those can't exceed any budget
Move every team to provisioned throughput so spend is fixed
Unity Gateway budgets with per-user thresholds, a blocking shared threshold and tags
questions.explanation: Budgets cover pay-per-token, AI Functions and Genie, with per-user daily or monthly thresholds and a shared threshold that can block. Tags enable cost analysis by team. Remember that enforcement is approximate, so set thresholds with headroom.

questions.question: A customer's production agent runs on provisioned throughput. They set a Unity Gateway budget, but the agent's spend doesn't show up in it. Why?
choices: Provisioned throughput is free
The budget needs 24 hours to activate before it starts tracking any provisioned spend
Budgets only track external models
Budgets don't cover provisioned throughput, which is billed hourly
questions.explanation: Budgets cover pay-per-token, AI Functions, Genie and optionally external models, not provisioned throughput or standalone serving endpoints. Manage provisioned throughput through sizing, reservations and utilization reviews instead.

questions.question: A customer's agent runs a classification step on every request using Claude Sonnet. Accuracy is fine on smaller models in tests. What's the cost advice?
choices: Keep Sonnet everywhere, since model choice has little effect on cost compared with warehouse compute and storage
Move the step to provisioned throughput on Sonnet
Route that step to a cheaper model through Unity Gateway after checking quality with MLflow
Switch the whole agent to priority pay-per-token
questions.explanation: Databricks' listed input rate for Sonnet is about six times Llama 3.3 70B's. Using evaluation to prove a smaller model is good enough, then switching the model in the gateway without code changes, is the standard optimization.

questions.question: A customer has a steady, high-volume agent with a latency SLA, plus spiky experimental workloads. How should they serve models?
choices: Pay-per-token for both, with priority mode always on so the SLA agent never waits behind experimental traffic
Provisioned throughput for both, sized for the experiments
Provisioned throughput for the steady SLA agent; pay-per-token for the spiky experiments
Custom GPU endpoints for both
questions.explanation: Provisioned throughput suits steady workloads with performance guarantees; pay-per-token suits variable or early workloads. Mixing both by workload is the usual pattern, and pay-per-token can be covered by budgets.

questions.question: A customer needs to extract fields from two million invoices every night. Which approach fits best?
choices: Copilot Studio agent flows, one flow per invoice
A Knowledge Assistant with every invoice uploaded
A chat agent that users ask to process each invoice one by one, with results copied into a table
A scheduled pipeline or job using ai_parse_document and ai_extract over the full dataset
questions.explanation: Document Intelligence functions are GA and built for batch. Submit the full dataset in one query and schedule it in Lakeflow or jobs; the AI Function job task (Beta) processes only new or changed inputs. A chat agent would be slower and more expensive for bulk work.

questions.question: A customer wants an HR policy assistant where managers see manager-only documents and employees don't. They plan one AI Search index. What's the risk and fix?
choices: Use a storage-optimized endpoint, which enforces document permissions
Put the instructions 'don't show manager documents' in the system prompt
No risk, because Unity Catalog row filters on the source table apply to index results automatically
AI Search has no row-level security, so use separate indexes per audience or enforce filters in the application
questions.explanation: AI Search indexes are governed by Unity Catalog, but row- and column-level permissions aren't supported. The docs recommend application-level filters. Prompt instructions are not a security boundary.

questions.question: A team's agent on Databricks Apps must respect row filters for each user. Testing shows everyone sees the same rows. What's the likely cause?
choices: Row filters don't apply to Databricks Apps under any circumstances, so a view must be created for each user group
App authorization is in use, or user authorization is silently falling back to the service principal
The users need a Premium Copilot license
The SQL warehouse is too small
questions.explanation: Per-user enforcement needs user authorization (Public Preview) with the right scopes, and get_user_workspace_client() called inside the handler. If the forwarded token is missing, it falls back to the service principal without error, so verify with a whoami tool.

questions.question: A customer wants their LangGraph agent to remember user preferences across sessions, governed like other data. Where should memory live?
choices: In the model's weights, through nightly fine-tuning
In Lakebase, registered in Unity Catalog
In the browser's local storage
In a spreadsheet on SharePoint
questions.explanation: Lakebase stores durable short- and long-term agent memory for LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK agents, and Databricks' agent memory service is built on it. Registering it in Unity Catalog brings memory under the same governance as data.

questions.question: A customer's agents need to read Jira tickets and SharePoint files. How can they keep that governed in Databricks?
choices: Give each agent the admin's personal API keys for Jira and SharePoint, stored in the agent's code
Use Databricks-managed MCP services registered in Unity Catalog, with Unity Gateway policies
It can't be governed; external tools are outside Databricks
Copy all Jira and SharePoint data into a public bucket
questions.explanation: Databricks lists managed MCP services for Jira, Confluence, SharePoint, Slack, GitHub and Google Drive. Registering them in Unity Catalog lets Unity Gateway apply permissions, usage tracking and (in Beta) contextual service policies.

questions.question: A customer wants a low-code agent that answers from both sales tables and PDF policy documents. Learn now labels Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent as legacy. What should they start with?
choices: A custom LangGraph agent written from scratch
Two separate tools with no connection between them
A new Knowledge Assistant plus a new Supervisor Agent, since legacy features still get new investment
A Genie Agent, using Agent mode for documents in volumes alongside structured data
questions.explanation: The legacy notices point new low-code document agents to Genie Agents. Genie's Agent mode adds volumes and MCP connectors to structured data. Go to code-based agents (Agent Bricks CLI) only when requirements outgrow that.

questions.question: A customer is choosing between Claude Enterprise and ChatGPT Enterprise for all 4,000 employees and asks whether that replaces Genie. What's the best coaching answer?
choices: No; Genie can't be used alongside any other assistant
Yes; general assistants enforce Unity Catalog permissions the same way Genie does, once connectors are configured
An assistant doesn't replace governed data answers; keep Genie for data and connect it through MCP
Yes, as long as users upload CSV exports into the assistant
questions.explanation: General assistants answer from connectors and uploads; Genie answers from governed tables with per-user Unity Catalog enforcement, metric views and benchmarks. Both Claude (custom MCP connectors) and Genie (MCP server, Conversation API) support integration, so it's 'and', not 'or'.

questions.question: A customer compares Snowflake Cortex Agents with Genie on cost. Which cost layers should they line up?
choices: Only per-seat prices, since both vendors include tokens and warehouse compute in a seat license
Nothing; both are free
Only storage costs
Model tokens (AI Credits vs Genie usage) plus warehouse compute for generated SQL on each side
questions.explanation: Snowflake bills Cortex Agents in AI Credits per million tokens with warehouse compute separate; Genie bills LLM usage beyond the free allowance with SQL compute separate. Compare like with like, including search or retrieval services.

questions.question: An internal Agentforce sales assistant will perform about 50,000 actions a month on Flex Credits. What's the monthly cost at list price?
choices: About $100,000, since every action is billed at the $2 per-conversation rate
About $2,000
About $5,000 (50,000 × 20 credits = 1 million credits at $500 per 100,000)
questions.explanation: Each action is 20 Flex Credits, so 50,000 actions use 1,000,000 credits. At $500 per 100,000 credits that's $5,000 a month, before any Data 360 consumption. Compare with $150 per user per month for unmetered add-ons when user counts are small and usage is heavy.

questions.question: A customer evaluating AWS Bedrock AgentCore says 'it's cheaper because there are no seats'. What should you point out?
choices: Costs come from many metered components (runtime, memory, gateway, models), so model each
AgentCore charges a flat fee per agent
AgentCore is free for all AWS customers with an Enterprise Support plan, apart from model token charges
AgentCore includes Copilot licenses
questions.explanation: AgentCore is consumption-based across Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Policy, Identity, Observability (CloudWatch), Evaluations and model usage. No seats doesn't mean low cost; estimate each meter. Data governance still needs a home, which Unity Catalog and Genie can provide.

questions.question: A customer wants a shared Copilot Studio agent to call Genie with one service principal for all users. What two concerns should you raise?
choices: Service principal usage is billed, and everyone gets the principal's data access
Service principals need a Microsoft 365 E5 license each
Service principals are free under the promotion, and they enforce each user's permissions automatically
Service principals can't call Genie at all
questions.explanation: Genie's free promotion excludes service principals, whose usage is billed. A shared principal also collapses per-user Unity Catalog enforcement. Prefer per-user OAuth paths where answers depend on who's asking.

questions.question: A customer wants to promote Genie Agents from dev to prod with review and rollback. What should you recommend?
choices: Rebuild each agent by hand in prod, since Genie Agents can't be exported, versioned or promoted between workspaces
Manage agents as code with bundles and the Genie management API, with benchmarks as a release gate
Share the dev agent with prod users
Export screenshots of the dev agent
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends deploying and versioning Genie Agents as code with bundles, and the management API supports CI/CD. Running benchmarks before promotion turns accuracy into a release gate.

questions.question: A customer's AI review board asks how to stop an agent from emailing PII outside the company while still letting it summarize PII internally. Which Databricks feature addresses this?
choices: Lakebase branching
AI Search full-text indexes
Unity Gateway Contextual Service Policies (Beta)
Genie benchmarks, which test agents against PII scenarios before they're deployed to production
questions.explanation: Contextual Service Policies decide per request based on user, agent, model, MCP service, tool and content. Databricks' own example blocks PII from publishing but allows it in email; the same mechanism can block outbound email. It's Beta, so set expectations.

questions.question: A CIO asks for the one-sentence case for Databricks as the agent platform when Microsoft 365 Copilot is already deployed. Which is most accurate?
choices: Keep Copilot as the front door; use Genie and Unity Catalog for governed, per-user data answers
Avoid integrating them, because Genie can't be called from Microsoft 365
Replace Copilot everywhere, because Genie writes Word documents better
Use Copilot for data questions, since it reads Unity Catalog permissions natively and applies row filters for each user
questions.explanation: Genie reaches users in Teams, Copilot and other front ends while answers stay governed by Unity Catalog with the asker's identity, benchmarks and metric views. Genie has no seats, and its usage is free for users through January 31, 2027. That positions Databricks as the governed data layer behind whichever assistant the customer chooses.

questions.question: Analysts want to ask plain-language questions over 12 curated sales tables and get answers that match certified metrics. Which Databricks option fits?
choices: A custom LangGraph agent served on Model Serving
An AI Search index built over the sales tables
A Genie Agent over those tables and their metric views
A Supervisor Agent with one subagent per table
questions.explanation: A Genie Agent is built for curated, domain-specific analytics: chosen tables (up to 50), metric views, instructions and example SQL. Metric views define metrics once so answers stay consistent. A custom agent or search index adds work without the governed NL-to-SQL Genie already provides.

questions.question: Executives want the same 12 KPIs every morning in a fixed layout, with occasional follow-up questions. What's the best fit?
choices: An AI/BI dashboard for the KPIs, with Genie alongside for follow-ups
AI Functions that summarize the KPI tables into a nightly email
A Genie Agent alone, asked the same 12 questions every morning
A Supervisor Agent that rebuilds the same KPIs from scratch in each conversation
questions.explanation: Fixed, repeated views belong in a dashboard: consistent, fast and cheap to run on a schedule. Genie shines at the follow-up 'why' and 'what about' questions. Using Genie for a fixed report adds model calls without adding value.

questions.question: A customer says, 'Copilot Studio can already query Databricks, so we don't need Genie.' What's the accurate reply?
choices: Copilot Studio's Databricks tool calls a Genie Agent, so Genie still answers the governed question
That's right: Copilot Studio writes and runs its own SQL against Unity Catalog without Genie
Copilot Studio can't reach Databricks at all, so Genie is the only way for Microsoft users to get there
Copilot Studio reaches Databricks only through Fabric mirroring, so Genie isn't involved
questions.explanation: The Azure Databricks Genie tool in Copilot Studio connects to a specific Genie Agent by ID. Copilot Studio handles the conversation and orchestration, and Genie turns the question into governed SQL under Unity Catalog. They're complementary, and the quality of the answer depends on how well the Genie Agent is curated.

questions.question: A 5,000-person company compares a $30 per user per month seat for everyone with Genie, where 600 people use about $15 of AI a month after a $10 allowance. What's the monthly AI cost of each, before compute?
questions.explanation: Seats: 5,000 × $30 = $150,000. Genie: 600 × ($15 − $10) = $3,000, plus warehouse compute. It isn't like for like, because a Copilot seat buys much more than data questions, but it shows why usage pricing suits tools that only some people use. Make that point fairly and it lands.
